faq.a: If pain starts before menses, lasts more than 3 days, is not relieved by NSAIDs, or is accompanied by fever, heavy bleeding, or a pelvic mass.
faq.q: When is menstrual pain considered abnormal?

faq.a: Yes; heat therapy, regular exercise, and dietary omega‑3 intake can modestly reduce pain, especially in primary dysmenorrhea.
faq.q: Can dysmenorrhea be treated without medication?

faq.a: Aspirin has weaker prostaglandin inhibition and higher risk of gastrointestinal bleeding, especially in patients with anemia or ulcer disease.

exam: What history points differentiate primary from secondary dysmenorrhea? — Look for pain onset before menses, duration > 3 days, dyspareunia, infertility, and heavy bleeding.

A 19‑year‑old with severe cramping pain unrelieved by ibuprofen and a tender uterus on exam. What is your next step? — Perform pelvic ultrasound (if available) or refer for specialist evaluation for possible secondary cause.
Why are NSAIDs preferred as first‑line therapy for primary dysmenorrhea? — They block prostaglandin synthesis, reducing uterine hypercontractility and pain.

In a patient with HIV presenting with cyclical pelvic pain, what additional investigation is essential? — STI screen (including chlamydia and gonorrhea) and urine microscopy for schistosome eggs if endemic.

How would you manage a patient with dysmenorrhea and hemoglobin 7 g/dL? — Start iron supplementation, treat any underlying cause of heavy bleeding, and consider referral for surgical management if fibroids are present.
What are red‑flag signs that require urgent referral? — Fever, vomiting, sudden severe pain, hemodynamic instability, or signs of severe anemia.
Explain why combined oral contraceptives can be used when NSAIDs fail. — They suppress ovulation, thin the endometrium, and reduce menstrual flow, decreasing prostaglandin release.

A woman reports pain that improves with heat and exercise but not with NSAIDs. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Primary dysmenorrhea with possible NSAID intolerance; consider non‑pharmacologic measures and alternative analgesics.
ai.title: Cyclical Abdominal Pain (Dysmenorrhea)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Recurrent pelvic or lower‑abdominal pain that coincides with the menstrual cycle. Common in low‑resource settings and may mask serious pathology. Management focuses on identifying primary versus secondary causes and providing affordable relief.

b: Primary dysmenorrhea: functional uterine prostaglandin excess, common in adolescents.
Secondary dysmenorrhea: endometriosis, adenomyosis, pelvic inflammatory disease, fibroids, ovarian cysts, or tubal pathology.
sections.p: Cyclical abdominal pain occurs at predictable points in the menstrual cycle, usually within 48 hours of onset of menses and lasting 1‑3 days. It is classified as primary (no underlying disease) or secondary (due to pelvic pathology).

b: Pain that starts before menses or persists > 3 days suggests secondary cause.
Associated symptoms – dyspareunia, dyschezia, infertility, heavy bleeding – point to endometriosis or fibroids.
In low‑resource settings, consider pelvic infection (TB, HIV‑related PID) and schistosomiasis.
sections.p: Understanding the pain pattern, associated symptoms and risk factors guides differentiation between primary and secondary causes.

b: Identify red‑flag features: fever, vomiting, sudden severe pain, anemia, or mass.
Early detection of secondary causes prevents infertility and chronic pain.
sections.p: Severe dysmenorrhea can impair school or work attendance and may be a marker for underlying disease that requires treatment.
When imaging is unavailable, rely on detailed history, bimanual exam, and response to analgesia to infer likely pathology.

t.b: Excludes early pregnancy as cause of abdominal pain — positive requires obstetric management.
Detects urinary tract infection or schistosome hematuria — treat accordingly.
Identifies fibroids, ovarian cysts, or fluid collections — guides surgical referral.
Assesses anemia from heavy bleeding; low hemoglobin suggests need for iron supplementation.

t.a: STI screen (HIV, syphilis, chlamydia) when risk factors present
t.b: Positive results indicate need for antimicrobial therapy and partner treatment.

b: If NSAID contraindicated or ineffective: low‑dose combined oral contraceptive (COC) – suppresses ovulation and stabilises endometrium.
Iron supplementation for anemia secondary to heavy menstrual bleeding.
Treat identified infection (e.g., metronidazole for bacterial vaginosis, doxycycline for chlamydia).
Refer for surgical evaluation when large fibroids, ovarian cysts, or suspected endometriosis are present.
sections.p: Treat primary dysmenorrhea with affordable analgesia and lifestyle measures; address secondary causes with targeted therapy or referral.

b: Ask timing relative to menses, duration, need for analgesia, and effect of NSAIDs.
Perform bimanual exam: assess uterine size, tenderness, adnexal masses.
Check for signs of anemia (pallor, tachycardia) and infection (fever, pelvic tenderness).
sections.p: Focus on pattern, severity, and associated features; use a systematic approach to avoid missing secondary causes.

b: Ignoring red‑flag symptoms such as fever or persistent pain beyond 3 days.
Prescribing NSAIDs without checking for renal disease or active GI ulcer.
Failing to consider pelvic infection in HIV‑positive or TB‑endemic patients.
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from assuming all menstrual pain is primary.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with vomiting
Heavy bleeding causing dizziness or fainting
Signs of anemia (hemoglobin < 8 g/dL) or shock
